answers.flag: Option D is a second, weakly defensible answer: AWS itself says base throughput is proportionate to Standard storage size (50 KiBps per each GiB) and a Lambda troubleshooting page says to 'increase the size of the file system or use provisioned throughput' when burst credits run out. The stem gives no storage price, no throughput figure and no amount of extra data, so a reader cannot prove from the stem that padding with data costs more than Provisioned throughput; the saved AWS pages carry no price per GiB or per MiBps to settle it. Option C is still the AWS-recommended fix for a throughput-constrained Bursting file system with predictable sustained load, and D only works at a stated cost that the stem does not give.

A.quote: Elastic Throughput is ideal if you’re unsure of your application’s peak throughput needs or if your application is very spiky, with a low baseline activity (such that it uses less than 5% of capacity on average when you provision for peak needs).
You pay only for the amount of metadata and data read or written, and you don't accrue or consume burst credits while using Elastic throughput.

B.quote: A file system's throughput mode determines the throughput available to your file system.
Max I/O mode is a previous generation performance type that is designed for highly parallelized workloads that can tolerate higher latencies than the General Purpose mode.

C.quote: With Provisioned throughput, you specify a level of throughput that the file system can drive independent of the file system's size or burst credit balance.
You should use Provisioned Throughput if you have predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements.

D.quote: If no burst credits are available, a file system can drive up to 50 MiBps per TiB of storage, with a minimum of 1 MiBps.
